learn: Everything around us is made of materials, like wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth.
A chair might be made of wood. A spoon might be made of metal.
One object can be made of more than one material: a pencil has wood, graphite, metal and rubber.
check: A spoon is often made of...
Can one object be made of more than one material?
lessons.try: Pick three objects and list the materials in each.

learn: Properties describe what a material is like.
Colour, texture, hardness, flexibility and whether it floats or sinks are properties.
Metal is hard and strong. Rubber is flexible and bouncy.
lessons.try: Test five objects to see which float and which sink in a bowl of water.

learn: Engineers choose materials whose properties fit the job.
A raincoat needs a waterproof material, like plastic. A window needs a transparent one, like glass.
Using the wrong material can make an object fail: a paper umbrella would get soggy.
check: A raincoat needs a material that is...
Why wouldn't a paper umbrella work?
A window needs a material that is...
lessons.try: Design a cup for hot cocoa. Which material would you choose and why?

learn: Wood comes from trees.
It is strong, it floats and it can be cut and shaped.
We use wood for houses, tables and pencils.
lessons.try: Find five wooden things in the room.

learn: Metal is hard, shiny and strong.
It lets heat and electricity pass through.
Pots, coins, nails and cars are made of metal.
lessons.try: Test which things a magnet sticks to.

learn: Plastic is made by people, mostly from oil.
It can be bendy or hard, and it is waterproof.
Too much plastic hurts oceans, so we reuse and recycle.
lessons.try: Sort plastic things into reusable and throwaway.

learn: Glass is made from melted sand.
It is hard, see-through and can break.
Windows, jars and lenses are glass.
lessons.try: List glass things at home and how to handle them safely.

learn: Fabric is cloth made from threads.
Cotton comes from plants. Wool comes from sheep.
Fabric is soft and bendy, good for clothes.
lessons.try: Feel three fabrics and describe them.

learn: Paper is made from wood pulp.
Cardboard is thick paper, strong but light.
Paper soaks up water. Cardboard gets soggy when wet.
lessons.try: Test paper towels for which soaks up most water.

learn: Rock is hard and heavy, good for walls.
Clay is soft wet earth that hardens when baked.
Bricks and pots are made from clay.
lessons.try: Make a small pot from clay and let it dry.

learn: Natural materials come from nature: wood, wool, stone.
Human-made materials are made by people: plastic, glass, steel.
Many things use both.
lessons.try: Sort twenty objects into natural and human-made.

learn: Use describing words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stiff.
Also: shiny, dull, heavy, light, see-through.
Exact words help scientists share.
lessons.try: Describe five objects with three words each.

learn: Some materials float: wood, cork, plastic foam.
Some sink: rock, metal, glass marbles.
Predict, then test in water.
lessons.try: Test ten objects in a tub of water.

learn: A spoon can be metal, wood or plastic.
Each material changes how it works.
A metal spoon gets hot in soup. A wooden spoon doesn't.
check: Which spoon gets hot in soup?
A spoon can be made of...
The material changes how the object...
lessons.try: Compare three spoons made of different materials.

learn: Every object is made of materials.
Each material has properties that make it good for some jobs.
Scientists test materials to choose the best one.
lessons.try: Make a materials poster.

learn: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.
A solid keeps its own shape. A block, a rock and an ice cube are solids.
A solid stays the same shape even if you put it in a different container.
check: Anything that takes up space and has mass
Takes the shape of its container
lessons.try: Put a block in a cup, then in a bowl. Did its shape change?

learn: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Water, milk and juice are liquids.
A liquid keeps the same amount even when poured into a different shape of container.
check: A liquid takes the shape of its...
When poured, the amount of liquid...
lessons.try: Pour one cup of water into a tall glass and then a wide bowl. Is it still one cup?

learn: A gas spreads out to fill whatever space it is in.
Air is a mix of gases. You can't see it, but you can feel it as wind.
Blowing up a balloon fills it with gas.
check: Spreads out to fill its space
What fills a balloon when you blow it up?
lessons.try: Blow up a balloon. What is inside it?

learn: Matter is anything that takes up space.
It comes in three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Ice, water and steam are all water in different states.
check: Matter is anything that takes up...
lessons.try: Draw ice, water and steam.

learn: A solid keeps its own shape.
A block stays a block in any box.
Solids can be hard or soft, like a rock or a pillow.
lessons.try: Move solids into different cups. Do they change shape?

lessons.t: Liquids Take the Shape of Containers
learn: A liquid flows and pours.
It takes the shape of whatever it is in.
Water, milk and honey are liquids.
check: A liquid takes the shape of its...
lessons.try: Pour water into three different containers.

learn: A gas spreads out to fill any space.
Most gases are invisible, like air.
You can feel air when the wind blows.
lessons.try: Blow up a balloon and talk about what's inside.

learn: Some liquids flow fast, like water. Some flow slowly, like honey.
Slow liquids are thick. Fast liquids are thin.
Race liquids down a tray.
lessons.try: Race water, syrup and oil down a tilted tray.

learn: Sand and sugar pour like liquids.
But each grain is a tiny solid that keeps its shape.
Look closely with a magnifier.
check: Each grain of sand is a...
Sugar can ___ but is a solid.
lessons.try: Look at sand under a hand lens.

learn: Air takes up space even though you can't see it.
Push an upside-down cup into water. The air keeps the inside dry.
Air pushes on things too.
check: The tissue stays dry because of...
lessons.try: Try the dry-tissue-in-a-cup trick.

learn: Water vapour is water as a gas.
It rises from puddles, kettles and our breath.
When it cools, it turns back into drops.
check: Water vapour is water as a...
Breath on a cold mirror makes...
lessons.try: Breathe on a cold mirror and watch the drops.

learn: Sort things by state: solid, liquid or gas.
Ask: Does it keep its shape? Does it pour? Does it spread out?
Some things are mixtures, like fizzy drinks.
lessons.try: Sort twenty picture cards into three groups.

learn: We measure liquids with cups, jugs and spoons.
Read the line at eye level.
Litres and cups are units for liquids.
check: A litre is a unit for...
lessons.try: Measure one cup of water.

learn: Matter can change from one state to another.
Heat melts ice into water. Cold freezes water into ice.
More heat turns water into steam.
lessons.try: Watch an ice cube melt and time it.

learn: Solids keep their shape. Liquids pour. Gases spread out.
Water can be all three.
Heating and cooling change states.
lessons.try: Act out solid, liquid and gas as a class.

learn: Heating a solid can make it melt into a liquid. Ice melts into water.
Cooling a liquid can make it freeze into a solid. Water freezes into ice.
Butter and chocolate melt when warm, too.
lessons.try: Put an ice cube on a plate in the sun and one in the shade. Which melts first?

learn: Some changes can be reversed. Melted ice can be frozen again.
Melted chocolate can harden again when it cools.
These are called reversible changes.
check: Can melted ice be frozen again?
A change that can be undone is...
Melted chocolate cooling and hardening is...
lessons.try: Freeze water in a tray, let it melt, then freeze it again.

learn: Some changes can't be reversed. You can't un-bake a cake or un-cook an egg.
Burning paper turns it into ash and smoke for good.
These are called irreversible changes. Cooking should always be done with a grown-up.
check: Who should be with you when cooking?
lessons.try: With a grown-up, cook an egg. Can it go back to raw?

learn: Heat makes things warmer.
The sun, fire and stoves give heat.
Heat can melt, cook and dry things.
lessons.try: Put butter in sun and in shade. Compare.

learn: Melting is a solid turning into a liquid.
Ice, chocolate and wax melt with heat.
Different things melt at different temperatures.
check: Melting turns a solid into a...
lessons.try: Race chocolate, butter and ice to melt in warm hands.

learn: Freezing is a liquid turning into a solid.
Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F).
Juice can freeze into ice pops.
check: Freezing turns a liquid into a...
lessons.try: Freeze juice and check every hour.

learn: Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas.
Puddles dry up because the water evaporates.
Heat and wind make evaporation faster.
check: Evaporation turns a liquid into a...
lessons.try: Mark a puddle with chalk and check it each hour.

learn: Condensation is a gas turning into a liquid.
Drops form on a cold glass on a hot day.
The water comes from the air, not through the glass.
check: Condensation turns a gas into a...
Drops on a cold glass come from the...
lessons.try: Put ice water in a glass and watch the outside.

learn: Water evaporates from seas, rises and cools.
It condenses into clouds, then falls as rain or snow.
The same water goes round and round.
lessons.try: Draw the water cycle with arrows.

learn: Melting and freezing can be undone.
Melt ice, then freeze it again. It's still water.
Reversible changes don't make a new material.
lessons.try: Melt and refreeze chocolate in a mould.

learn: Cooking an egg can't be undone.
Burning paper makes ash and smoke. You can't make paper again.
These changes make new materials.
lessons.try: Compare a raw egg and a cooked egg.

learn: Baking turns batter into cake.
Heat makes bubbles and sets the cake.
You can't turn cake back into flour and eggs.
check: Baking is a change you ___ reverse.
lessons.try: Look at batter and a baked cake. List the changes.

learn: Hot things can burn skin.
Use oven mitts and ask an adult near stoves and fires.
Never touch a hot pan handle without checking.
lessons.try: Make a heat safety poster.

learn: Insulators slow heat: wool, foam and cool boxes.
Wrap ice in a cloth and it melts slower.
Thermoses keep drinks hot or cold.
lessons.try: Wrap ice cubes in different materials and time melting.

learn: Heat melts and evaporates. Cold freezes and condenses.
Some changes reverse and some don't.
Always be safe with heat.
check: A solid becoming a liquid is...
lessons.try: Play the change match game.

learn: Large objects can be built from many small pieces.
A wall is made of many bricks. A house can be built from logs or blocks.
Toy blocks can be built into a tower, then taken apart and built into a bridge.
check: What is a wall made of?
Can the same pieces build different things?
A tower of blocks can become a...
lessons.try: Build something with blocks, then take it apart and build something new.

learn: When you take an object apart, you can see its pieces.
A puzzle is many pieces that fit together.
Scientists take things apart to learn how they work.
check: Why do scientists take things apart?
When you take an object apart, you see its...
lessons.try: With a grown-up, look at the parts of an old pen or a toy.

learn: A structure is something built to hold weight or stand up.
Wide bases make towers more stable. Triangles make structures strong.
Engineers test their structures and improve them.
check: What makes a tower more stable?
lessons.try: Build a paper tower that can hold a book. Test and improve it.

learn: Big things are often built from small pieces.
A tower can be built from many blocks.
The same blocks can build different things.
check: Big things can be built from...
A tower can be built from...
lessons.try: Build a house and then a bridge from the same blocks.

learn: Walls are made of many bricks.
Bricks overlap so the wall is strong.
Mortar glues bricks together.
check: Bricks ___ to make a strong wall.
A wall is made of many...
lessons.try: Build a wall with overlapping blocks and test it.

learn: A puzzle is many pieces making one picture.
Every piece has a place.
Missing pieces leave gaps.
check: A puzzle is many pieces making one...
lessons.try: Make a ten-piece puzzle from a drawing.

learn: Take apart a block model and build something new.
The pieces are the same, but the shape is different.
Nothing is lost when you rebuild.
check: When you rebuild, the pieces are the...
The new object has a different...
lessons.try: Take apart a model and rebuild it as something new.

learn: A whole weighs the same as all its parts.
Weigh a block tower, take it apart, and weigh the pieces.
The total weight stays the same.
check: A whole weighs the ___ as its parts.
Taking a tower apart changes its weight?
lessons.try: Weigh a tower and its parts on a scale.

learn: Sand dunes are made of tiny grains.
Beaches, deserts and sandcastles are made of sand.
Nature builds big things from small pieces too.
check: Sand dunes are made of tiny...
lessons.try: Build a sandcastle and look at its grains.

learn: Birds build nests from twigs, grass and mud.
Bees build hives from wax cells.
Animals are builders too.
lessons.try: Build a nest from twigs and grass.

learn: Triangles make structures strong.
Bridges and roofs use triangles.
Squares can squash, but triangles hold their shape.
lessons.try: Build a square and a triangle with straws and push them.

learn: Wide bases make towers stable.
Narrow bases make towers tip over.
Heavy pieces belong at the bottom.
lessons.try: Build two towers with wide and narrow bases. Test them.

learn: Engineers build with limited materials.
Use only paper and tape to build the tallest tower.
Test, improve and try again.
check: Rolling paper into tubes makes it...
lessons.try: Build the tallest tower from 10 sheets of paper.

learn: Test a structure by adding weight bit by bit.
Count how many coins or books it holds.
Record your results in a chart.
check: A fair test changes ___ thing at a time.
lessons.try: Test a paper bridge with pennies.

learn: Big things are made from small pieces.
Pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt.
Shape and base change a structure's strength.
check: A whole weighs the ___ as its parts.
lessons.try: Show your strongest model to the class.

learn: Plants need sunlight to make their food.
A plant in a dark closet will turn yellow and weak.
Plants often bend toward light.
check: What do plants need sunlight for?
A plant in the dark turns...
lessons.try: Put a plant near a window and watch it lean toward the light over a week.

learn: Plants need water. Roots take water from the soil.
Too little water makes plants wilt. Too much can rot roots.
Soil gives plants nutrients and holds them steady.
check: What do roots take from the soil?
What happens with too little water?
lessons.try: Grow two bean seeds: water one, don't water the other. Compare.

learn: Plants need air and room to grow.
Leaves take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide.
Crowded plants compete for light, water and space.
check: What gas do leaves take from the air?
Do plants need room to grow?
lessons.try: Plant seeds close together and far apart. Which grow better?

learn: Plants have roots, stems, leaves and flowers.
Roots hold the plant and drink water. Stems carry water up.
Leaves make food. Flowers make seeds.
lessons.try: Label a real plant's parts.

learn: Grow one plant in a sunny window and one in a dark cupboard.
The dark plant turns pale and weak.
Plants need light to make food.
check: A plant in the dark turns...
lessons.try: Set up a light and dark plant test.

learn: Water one plant and don't water another.
The dry plant wilts and droops.
Too much water can rot roots.
check: Plants need the ___ amount of water.
lessons.try: Water two plants differently for a week.

learn: Soil holds roots and gives nutrients.
Nutrients are like vitamins for plants.
Compost adds nutrients to soil.
lessons.try: Compare a plant in rich soil and one in sand.

learn: Leaves take in air through tiny holes.
Plants use air, water and light to make food.
Plants give out oxygen we breathe.
check: To make food, plants need light, water and...
lessons.try: Look at a leaf under a hand lens.

learn: Plants need space for roots and leaves.
Crowded plants compete for light and water.
Gardeners thin out seedlings.
lessons.try: Plant beans close and far apart. Compare.

learn: Most plants grow best when it's warm, not too hot or cold.
Frost can kill tender plants.
Greenhouses keep plants warm.
check: Most plants grow best when it's...
lessons.try: Put a seed tray in a warm and a cool place.

learn: Plants bend toward the light.
A plant on a windowsill leans toward the window.
Turn it, and it bends back.
check: A windowsill plant leans toward the...
lessons.try: Watch a plant on the windowsill for a week.

learn: Roots grow down, even if a seed is upside down.
Stems grow up toward light.
Watch it in a clear cup with paper towel.
check: A clear cup lets you see the...
lessons.try: Grow a bean in a clear cup and watch the roots.

learn: In a fair test, change only one thing.
Keep the same pot, soil and seed. Change only water.
Then you know what caused the difference.
check: To test water, keep the ___ the same.
Fair tests show what ___ the difference.
lessons.try: Plan a fair test on plant food.

learn: Scientists keep journals of what they see.
Draw and measure your plant each week.
Write the date and what changed.
lessons.try: Start a plant journal.

learn: Plants need light, water, air, nutrients, space and warmth.
Without them, plants wilt or die.
Fair tests show what plants need.
lessons.try: Make a "what plants need" poster.

learn: Flowers make pollen, a yellow powder.
Bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and bats carry pollen from flower to flower.
Moving pollen helps flowers make seeds. This is pollination.
lessons.try: Watch a flowering plant for five minutes. What visitors come?

learn: Seeds travel to new places to grow.
Dandelion seeds float on the wind. Burrs stick to animal fur. Coconuts float on water.
Animals eat fruits and drop the seeds far away.
lessons.try: Blow on a dandelion and watch the seeds travel.

learn: Scientists build models to understand how things work.
You can model a bee with a pipe cleaner: dip it in one flower's powder and touch another flower.
The model shows how pollen moves.
check: In the model, the cotton swab is like a...
lessons.try: Use a cotton swab and cocoa powder to model pollination between two paper flowers.

learn: A seed has a baby plant inside, plus stored food.
A tough seed coat protects it.
Soak a bean and split it open to see the tiny plant.
check: Inside a seed is a baby...
lessons.try: Open a soaked bean and find the baby plant.

learn: Germination is when a seed starts to grow.
Seeds need water and warmth to germinate.
First a root comes out, then a shoot.
check: When a seed starts to grow it is called...
lessons.try: Germinate seeds in a wet paper towel bag.

learn: Flowers have petals, pollen and a centre where seeds grow.
Bright petals attract insects.
Pollen is a yellow powder.
lessons.try: Look closely at a flower and draw its parts.

learn: Pollination moves pollen from one flower to another.
Then the flower can make seeds.
Without pollination, many plants can't make fruit.
check: Without pollination, many plants can't make...
lessons.try: Use a cotton swab to move pollen between flowers.

learn: Bees drink nectar and carry pollen on fuzzy bodies.
Butterflies sip nectar with long tongues.
Both help flowers make seeds.
lessons.try: Watch a flower bed and count visitors.

learn: Hummingbirds pollinate red tube-shaped flowers.
Bats pollinate flowers that open at night.
Different animals visit different flowers.
check: Bats visit flowers that open at...
lessons.try: Match pollinators to their flowers.

learn: Some plants use wind to carry pollen.
Grasses, corn and pine trees are wind-pollinated.
Their flowers are small and plain.
lessons.try: Shake a grass flower over black paper and look for pollen.

learn: Dandelion seeds have fluffy parachutes.
Maple seeds spin like helicopters.
Wind carries them far away.
lessons.try: Make a paper helicopter like a maple seed.

learn: Burrs have hooks that stick to fur and socks.
Animals carry them far away.
Velcro was invented by copying burrs.
lessons.try: Walk through a field wearing old socks and look at what sticks.

learn: Animals eat fruit and drop the seeds elsewhere.
Squirrels bury nuts and forget some, which grow into trees.
Animals are seed gardeners.
lessons.try: Find seeds in an apple, a tomato and a strawberry.

learn: Coconuts float across oceans.
Water plants drop seeds that drift away.
Water carries seeds to new places.
check: A floating seed is light and...
lessons.try: Test which seeds float in water.

learn: Pollinators move pollen so plants make seeds.
Seeds travel by wind, water, animals and hooks.
We need pollinators for many foods.
lessons.try: Design a model seed that travels far.

learn: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives.
It gives the living thing food, water and shelter.
Different living things need different habitats.
check: A habitat gives food, water and...
Do all living things need the same habitat?
lessons.try: Choose an animal and draw its habitat.

learn: Deserts are dry. Camels and cactuses live there.
Rainforests are wet and warm with many kinds of life, like monkeys and frogs.
Oceans are salty water homes for whales, fish and coral. Polar areas are icy, home to polar bears and penguins.
check: Which habitat is wet and warm with many kinds of life?
lessons.try: Sort animal pictures into desert, rainforest, ocean and polar.

learn: Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place.
Some habitats, like rainforests, have huge biodiversity.
Scientists count and compare the living things in different places.
lessons.try: Count the different kinds of plants and bugs in a small patch of yard.

learn: Forests have many trees and shady floors.
Deer, owls, squirrels and bears live there.
Trees give food and shelter.
check: Which animal lives in a forest?
lessons.try: Make a forest diorama in a shoebox.

learn: Rainforests are hot and wet all year.
More kinds of living things live there than anywhere else on land.
Monkeys, frogs, parrots and jaguars live there.
lessons.try: Draw rainforest layers from floor to canopy.

learn: Deserts get very little rain.
Cactuses store water. Camels can go days without drinking.
Many desert animals come out at night when it's cool.
check: Many desert animals come out at...
lessons.try: Compare a cactus and a leafy plant.

learn: Polar lands are icy and cold.
Polar bears live in the Arctic. Penguins live in Antarctica.
Thick fur, fat and feathers keep them warm.
lessons.try: Feel how fat keeps you warm with a lard glove test.

learn: Oceans cover most of Earth.
Fish, whales, crabs and coral live there.
Ocean water is salty.
lessons.try: Taste-test fresh and salty water (just a drop).

learn: Ponds and rivers have fresh water.
Frogs, ducks, fish and dragonflies live there.
Rivers flow. Ponds stay still.
lessons.try: Look at pond water under a magnifier.

learn: Grasslands are wide, flat lands covered in grass.
Zebras, lions and bison live there.
There are few trees.
lessons.try: Make a grassland food chain.

learn: Mountains are high, cold and windy at the top.
Mountain goats climb steep rocks. Eagles nest on cliffs.
Fewer plants grow near the top.
check: Near mountain tops there are ___ plants.
lessons.try: Draw a mountain with zones from bottom to top.

learn: Animals have body parts that fit where they live.
Ducks have webbed feet for swimming. Camels have wide feet for sand.
These are called adaptations.
check: Body parts that fit a habitat are...
Wide feet help camels walk on...
lessons.try: Invent an animal for a habitat and draw its adaptations.

learn: Biodiversity means many kinds of living things.
Some habitats have more kinds than others.
Count kinds in a small square of schoolyard.
check: Biodiversity means many ___ of living things.
You can count kinds in a...
lessons.try: Count kinds of living things in a hoop on the grass.

learn: Cutting forests and polluting water harms habitats.
When habitats are lost, animals lose homes.
Protecting habitats protects animals.
check: When habitats are lost, animals lose...
lessons.try: Make a poster to protect a habitat.

learn: Habitats give food, water and shelter.
Each habitat has animals and plants adapted to it.
We can protect habitats.
lessons.try: Play habitat match: animal to home.

learn: Earth has many landforms: mountains, hills, valleys, plains, canyons and islands.
A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.
Maps can show where landforms are.
check: A deep valley with steep sides is a...
What can show where landforms are?
lessons.try: Model a mountain and a valley with sand or clay.

learn: Oceans are salt water. Most lakes and rivers are fresh water.
Water on Earth can be liquid or solid, like glaciers and ice caps.
Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
check: A glacier is water as a...
Where is most of Earth's water?
lessons.try: Taste a drop of salt water and a drop of fresh water (with a grown-up).

lessons.t: Making Maps of Land and Water
learn: Maps use colours and symbols: blue for water, green for low land, brown for mountains.
A map key explains the colours.
You can model a place and then draw its map from above.
check: What colour often shows water on a map?
What explains the colours on a map?
A map shows a place from...
lessons.try: Draw a map of a pretend island with a mountain, a lake and a river.

learn: Mountains are very high land with steep sides.
Hills are lower and rounder.
Both are landforms.
lessons.try: Make a mountain and a hill from clay.

learn: A valley is low land between hills or mountains.
A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.
The Grand Canyon was carved over millions of years.
check: The Grand Canyon took ___ to form.
lessons.try: Pour water down a sand slope and watch a valley form.

learn: Plains are wide, flat, low land.
Plateaus are flat land that is high up.
Farms are often on plains.
lessons.try: Build a plain and a plateau from clay.

learn: An island has water all around it.
A peninsula has water on three sides.
Florida is a peninsula. Hawaii is made of islands.
check: A peninsula has water on ___ sides.
lessons.try: Find islands and peninsulas on a map.

learn: Oceans are huge bodies of salt water.
Earth has five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern.
The Pacific is the biggest.
check: How many oceans does Earth have?
lessons.try: Colour the five oceans on a world map.

learn: Rivers are flowing fresh water that move toward the sea.
Small streams join to make big rivers.
The Mississippi is a long river in the United States.
lessons.try: Trace a river on a map from source to sea.

learn: Lakes are big bodies of water with land all around.
Ponds are smaller and shallower.
The Great Lakes hold lots of fresh water.
lessons.try: Find the Great Lakes on a map.

learn: Some water is frozen in glaciers and ice sheets.
Glaciers are huge rivers of ice that move slowly.
Antarctica is covered in an ice sheet.
lessons.try: Watch an ice cube slide slowly on a tray.

learn: Maps use colours and symbols.
Blue usually means water. Green means low land. Brown means high land.
The key explains the symbols.
lessons.try: Read the key on a physical map.

learn: Draw a map of the schoolyard from above, like a bird.
Add a key and symbols.
Show land and water features.
check: A map shows a place from...
lessons.try: Make a map of your schoolyard with a key.

learn: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
Only a little is fresh water we can drink.
Fresh water is in rivers, lakes, ice and underground.
check: Fresh water is ___ of Earth's water.
lessons.try: Show Earth's water with 100 beads: 97 blue, 3 white.

learn: Landforms include mountains, valleys, plains, islands and peninsulas.
Water forms include oceans, rivers, lakes and glaciers.
Maps show them with symbols.
check: Low land between mountains is a...
A huge body of salt water is an...
lessons.try: Play landform charades.

learn: Some changes to Earth take a very long time.
Wind and water slowly wear rock away. This is weathering and erosion.
The Grand Canyon was carved by a river over millions of years.
check: Wearing rock away by wind and water is...
Do these changes take a long time?
lessons.try: Rub two rocks together. Look at the dust: that's what weathering makes.

learn: Some changes happen quickly.
Earthquakes shake the ground. Volcanoes erupt with lava. Floods and landslides move land fast.
These events can change land in minutes or hours.
check: What comes out of an erupting volcano?
lessons.try: Make a model landslide by tilting a tray of wet sand.

learn: People design ways to slow down erosion.
Planting grass and trees holds soil in place with their roots.
Walls and fences can block wind and water.
check: What can block wind and water?
lessons.try: Test: pour water on bare soil and on soil with grass. Which washes away more?

learn: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces.
Water, ice, wind and plant roots can break rocks.
It usually takes a long time.
lessons.try: Shake sugar cubes in a jar and watch them wear down.

learn: Erosion moves broken bits of rock and soil away.
Rivers, wind and glaciers carry them.
Erosion can shape valleys and beaches.
lessons.try: Pour water on a sand hill and watch it erode.

learn: Wind blows sand into dunes.
It can carve rocks into arches over many years.
Wind erosion is strongest in dry places.
check: Wind erosion is strongest in ___ places.
lessons.try: Blow through a straw at sand and watch it move.

learn: Rivers carve canyons and valleys.
Waves wear away cliffs.
Rain washes soil down hills.
lessons.try: Build a model river in a tray of sand.

learn: Glaciers scrape rocks as they slide.
Water freezes in cracks and splits rocks.
Ice carved many lakes and valleys.
check: Water freezing in cracks can ___ rocks.
lessons.try: Freeze a water-filled balloon in clay and see the cracks.

learn: A volcano is an opening where hot melted rock comes out.
The melted rock is called lava.
Eruptions can make new land quickly.
check: Melted rock from a volcano is...
lessons.try: Make a baking soda volcano model.

learn: An earthquake is a shaking of the ground.
It happens when big pieces of Earth's crust slip.
Earthquakes can crack roads and buildings in seconds.
lessons.try: Build a block tower on a tray and shake it.

learn: Floods happen when too much water overflows rivers.
Landslides are rocks and soil sliding down hills fast.
Both can change land in hours.
lessons.try: Make a mini landslide on a wet sand slope.

learn: Some changes are fast: volcanoes, earthquakes, floods.
Some are slow: weathering, erosion, glaciers.
Sort changes by speed.
check: A canyon forming is a ___ change.
lessons.try: Sort ten Earth change cards into fast and slow.

learn: Plant roots hold soil in place.
Grass on hills stops soil washing away.
Trees by rivers protect riverbanks.
lessons.try: Pour water on bare soil and on grassy soil. Compare.

learn: People build walls to stop waves wearing away beaches.
Dams control rivers and floods.
Engineers design ways to protect land.
lessons.try: Design a sea wall for a sand beach model.

learn: Earth changes fast with volcanoes, earthquakes and floods.
It changes slowly with weathering and erosion.
People can help protect land.
lessons.try: Make a fast/slow change poster.

learn: Engineers start by asking: what is the problem? Who has it?
They list what the solution must do.
For example: "The plant tips over. We need a pot that stays up."
check: Engineers list what the solution must...
Who has the problem is part of...
lessons.try: Find a small problem at home and describe it clearly.

learn: Engineers sketch many ideas before they build.
Labels show the parts and materials.
Sharing sketches with others brings more ideas.
lessons.try: Sketch two ideas for solving your problem. Label them.

learn: Build your best idea and test it.
Compare two designs fairly: test them the same way.
Use what you learn to improve your design.
check: How should you compare two designs?
What do you do after testing?
lessons.try: Build two paper boats and test which holds more pennies.

learn: Engineers design things that solve problems.
Bridges, toys, shoes and phones were all designed.
Anyone can think like an engineer.
lessons.try: List five things engineers designed in the classroom.

learn: Engineers start by asking questions.
Who has the problem? What do they need? What's hard about it?
Good questions lead to good solutions.
check: Which is a good engineer question?
lessons.try: Interview a classmate about a problem they have.

learn: Every design has limits, like money, time and materials.
"Use only 10 straws" is a limit.
Limits make engineers creative.
check: Limits can be time, money or...
lessons.try: Build a bridge using only 10 straws and tape.

learn: Brainstorming means coming up with many ideas.
No idea is silly during brainstorming.
More ideas give more chances to find a great one.
lessons.try: Brainstorm ten ways to keep a lunch cold.

learn: A sketch is a quick drawing of your idea.
Label the parts and materials.
Sketches help others understand your idea.
lessons.try: Sketch a design for a pencil holder with labels.

learn: Compare ideas against the problem and limits.
Ask: Which works best? Which uses fewer materials?
Teams vote or combine ideas.
lessons.try: Pick your team's best design and explain why.

learn: A model is a small version of a design.
Build it to see if your idea works.
Models save time and money.
check: Models help see if an idea...
lessons.try: Build a model of your pencil holder.

learn: Test your model to see how well it works.
Measure and record what happens.
Test more than once.
check: Test to see how well a design...
lessons.try: Test your model three times and record results.

learn: Failure is part of engineering.
When something breaks, you learn why.
Famous inventors failed many times before succeeding.
lessons.try: Share a time something you built failed and what you learned.

learn: After testing, change your design to make it better.
Change one thing at a time and test again.
This loop is called iteration.
lessons.try: Improve your model and retest.

learn: Engineers share designs with others.
Show your model, results and what you changed.
Feedback helps you improve more.
check: Share your results and what you...
lessons.try: Present your design to the class.

learn: Ask, imagine, plan, build, test and improve.
Limits make design a challenge.
Failure helps you learn.
check: A quick drawing of an idea is a...
lessons.try: Make a poster of the engineering steps.
